That window is hard because 'stay seated' is an instruction about what not to do, and by ten to the class has already mentally left. It tends to work for a week because it's a rule, not a routine. A few things that usually hold better:

1. Give the last ten minutes a job with an end point. A short exit ticket (two or three questions on the lesson), a recall quiz, or 'one thing you'd tell next year's class' that you collect at the door. If they're working until the bell, there's nothing to pack up for.
2. Move packing up earlier and make it a controlled step. Say 'books away at five to, bags stay under desks, I'll dismiss you by table.' Then do dismissal by table or row, quietest first. That gives them a reward for settling and a reason to stay in place.
3. Tell them the rule once, with the reason, and then run the same sequence every lesson. The Friday-last-period class needs the sequence to be boring and identical more than it needs a stronger consequence.
4. Don't talk over the noise. Stand still, wait for quiet, then give a single instruction. If a few stand at the door, calmly send them back to their seat and restart the sequence without a lecture.

If you tell me roughly how the lesson usually ends (practical, notes, review), I can suggest a specific closing activity that fits.

You're not doing anything terrible, and it's good that you're taking his crying seriously. But I think the approach has drifted into something that's making the problem bigger.

Ten weeks is very young. Two to three hours of crying a night is a lot, and it suggests he's not yet comfortable being alone, and that going in and sitting with him has become part of how he falls asleep. Because settling takes ages, he's learning that crying is how to get you, and he's getting more practice each night. That can make it worse even though you've been consistent.

Things to try:
- Move the crate into your bedroom, near the bed, for now. Being able to hear and smell you matters a lot at this age. You can move it out gradually later.
- Tire him out in the evening, with a last toilet trip right before bed. Pups this age often need to go out once or twice in the night, so a cry at 2am may be a real need. Take him out calmly, no play, and straight back in.
- Build a short, boring bedtime routine, and give him something to chew or a warm (not hot) wrapped bottle or a worn t-shirt with your smell.
- Instead of sitting with him until he's asleep, sit near the crate and then move a little further away over several nights. Reward calm moments, not crying. A hand on the crate or a quiet word is fine.
- Practise short, happy crate time in the daytime with treats, so the crate isn't only about being left.

I wouldn't leave him to cry it out at this age. If he's still distressed after a week or so of changes, or he's not eating or toileting well, check in with your vet or a qualified trainer. Expect progress to be wobbly, but with these changes most pups improve within a week or two.

Good thing to check. The main combinations to keep apart:

- Bleach and ammonia (found in some glass cleaners and many urine or pet-stain products): produces chloramine vapours, which irritate the lungs and can cause coughing, chest pain and shortness of breath.
- Bleach and acids (vinegar, toilet bowl cleaners, some limescale removers): releases chlorine gas, which is toxic to breathe.
- Bleach and rubbing alcohol: can form chloroform and other harmful compounds.
- Different drain cleaners, or drain cleaner and anything else: can react violently, heat up and splatter or release fumes.
- Hydrogen peroxide and vinegar in the same container: forms peracetic acid, which is corrosive to skin, eyes and lungs.
- Baking soda and vinegar in a sealed container: not toxic, but it makes gas that can burst the container, and the mix cancels out the cleaning effect anyway.

Storage tips: keep products in their original labelled containers, never decant into food or drink bottles, keep bleach and acid-based products on separate shelves, store them out of reach of children and pets in a cool, ventilated spot, and never mix products 'to make them stronger'. If you ever do get fumes, leave and get fresh air immediately, and call poison control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) or your local emergency number if anyone has symptoms.

What you're describing is very common, and it isn't a sign something's wrong with you. After four years of caring for your mum at home, the relief of being able to sleep, of having a quiet house and not being on call, is real and earned. Eleven hours of sleep says a lot about how much you were carrying.

Feeling relieved doesn't mean you love her less or that you did the wrong thing. You can feel relief and sadness about the same event, sometimes at different times. Some people feel grief later, in a week or a month, and some mainly feel relief and settle into a new way of caring that works better for everyone. None of those is the wrong response.

As for telling people it was a hard day, that's a fine thing to say if you don't feel like going into more. You don't owe anyone a particular emotion. But it can help to have one person you can be honest with, who won't judge, so you aren't acting a feeling you don't have.

Please don't stop it on your own before you've spoken with your doctor or pharmacist. Your worry is based on something real, but the picture is less alarming than it sounds.

Long-term metformin use can lower vitamin B12 levels in some people, and low B12 can cause nerve problems if it's missed for a long time. But it's well known, easy to check with a blood test, and treatable with supplements or injections, and when caught early the nerve effects are usually preventable or reversible. Meanwhile, uncontrolled high blood sugar carries serious risks of its own, including nerve damage, kidney and eye problems and heart disease, and stopping suddenly can let those rise.

What I'd suggest:
- Tell your doctor what you've read and ask whether you should have your B12 checked now and at regular intervals (many guidelines recommend this for people on metformin, especially long term).
- Ask about tingling, numbness or unusual tiredness, and report any right away.
- If you really don't want to continue, ask about alternatives. There are other medicines, but it should be a decision made with them.

If you have numbness, tingling or balance problems now, tell your doctor soon rather than waiting for the next appointment.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. Having pay stubs is a strong start. Here's a general overview, though I'm not a lawyer and an employment attorney should look at your facts.

Laws that may apply:
- Equal Pay Act (federal): requires equal pay for substantially equal work regardless of sex. You can file a lawsuit directly in court, generally within 2 years of a underpayment (3 if willful), and you don't have to go through the EEOC first.
- Title VII of the Civil Rights Act: prohibits pay discrimination based on sex and race. You'd normally file a charge with the EEOC first. In Texas the deadline is typically 300 days from the discriminatory act, but under the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act each discriminatory paycheck can restart the clock.
- 42 U.S.C. section 1981: covers race discrimination in contracts, including employment, without an EEOC step and with a longer time limit (usually 4 years).
- Texas Labor Code Chapter 21: the state equivalent, enforced by the Texas Workforce Commission Civil Rights Division, with a shorter filing window (180 days), so some people file with both the EEOC and TWC.

Practical steps:
1. Keep your pay stubs and write down dates, job titles, duties and who your comparators are, and what each does.
2. Keep copies outside work systems, and note anything said about pay or why.
3. Know that retaliation for raising pay concerns or filing a charge is illegal, and in most private workplaces you may legally discuss pay with coworkers.
4. Talk to an employment discrimination attorney. Many give a free first consultation and some work on contingency. The EEOC (1-800-669-4000) and local legal aid or bar referral services can also help.

Given the deadlines, it's worth acting in the next few weeks. I can help you organise a timeline of your pay and a comparison chart to bring to a lawyer.

I can't look up registers or the landlord's records from here, so I can't tell you for certain whether he protected it. But you can check this yourself quickly, and I can tell you what it means for what you're owed. I'm assuming this is an assured shorthold tenancy in England.

How to check:
- Landlords must put a deposit in one of three schemes: the Deposit Protection Service (DPS), MyDeposits, or Tenancy Deposit Scheme (TDS). Each has a free 'find a deposit' search, using your name, postcode or the tenancy details. Try all three.
- The landlord must protect the deposit within 30 days of receiving it and give you the scheme details and prescribed information within that time. Not getting any paperwork is a strong sign he didn't.

If it was protected: the scheme runs a free dispute process, and you can ask them to get your deposit back, and the landlord has to respond or the scheme can release it to you if he doesn't engage.

If it wasn't protected: you can apply to the county court for your deposit back and for compensation of between one and three times the deposit, so potentially £900 to £2,700 on top of the £900 itself, depending on the judge. You'd normally send a formal letter before action first.

Steps: 1) run the three searches and screenshot results; 2) send a formal written demand (email and post) giving 14 days to return the deposit and noting his obligations; 3) if not, file a money claim online (a few tens to a couple of hundred pounds in fees, recoverable if you win). Keep the tenancy agreement, bank proof of payment and your emails. Shelter and Citizens Advice can also help, and I can write the demand letter if you give me his name, the address and dates.

Your instinct that something is wrong here is right. The churches' response isn't paranoia, it's a reasonable reaction to a real history (Tuskegee and many other cases), and your supervisor's plan to stop mentioning the research partnership would turn that history into a present-day problem.

Why I wouldn't go along with it:
- If the programme is research, people are entitled to know that, because it affects what happens to their data and what they are agreeing to. Leaving it out would likely breach informed consent rules and might breach the terms of your IRB approval.
- It would probably come out eventually, through a consent form, a news story or someone in the congregation. At that point you'd confirm the exact suspicion they've voiced, and lose trust for this programme and for future health work.
- It would put you in the position of deceiving people you're trying to help.

What I'd do instead:
1. Tell your supervisor, calmly, that being open is both the ethical and the practical option, and ask them to check with the IRB or university partner about what has to be disclosed. Put it in writing.
2. Go back to the churches with honesty: 'This is a partnership with the university. Here's exactly what data is collected, who sees it, that nothing experimental is being done to you, that you can say no and still get your screening, and that you can withdraw.' Having the real details in plain language on one page helps.
3. Ask pastors and church health ministry leaders to help shape it, and invite them into a community advisory role. Trusted Black physicians or local community health workers can also speak to the congregations.
4. Acknowledge the history directly instead of avoiding it. You could say 'You're right to ask, and we want you to be able to check us.'

Yes, a few things are worth doing before you start reading it. Land acknowledgments can mean something, or they can feel like a formality, and the difference is mostly in the care taken.

No. The best available evidence doesn't support the idea that women are naturally less suited to leadership. Large studies and meta-analyses of leadership effectiveness find that men and women perform about equally well, and where there are small differences they tend to point in different directions depending on the setting and what is measured. Some research finds women score slightly higher on things like collaborative and transformational leadership styles, which are linked to good outcomes, while differences in assertiveness are small and overlap heavily.

What clearly does differ is how women are treated. Women are underrepresented in leadership in most countries, and research points to causes such as stereotypes (assertive women are penalised more than assertive men), unequal caregiving expectations, bias in hiring and promotion, and fewer sponsors or role models. When those barriers are reduced, for example through structured hiring, the representation gap narrows. Countries and organisations with more women in leadership have not done worse.

Individual variation within each sex is much larger than any average difference between them, so sex is a poor predictor of who will lead well. If you're asking because of a particular argument you've encountered or a decision you're facing, I'm happy to look at that more specifically.

What fentanyl does: Fentanyl is a very strong opioid. Opioids act on receptors in the brain that control pain, but also the brain's drive to breathe. In an overdose, they overwhelm that drive.

How it typically progresses:
1. Drowsiness and slowed responses. The person becomes very sleepy, may seem to nod off, and may be hard to rouse. Pupils often become very small.
2. Slowed, shallow breathing. Breathing becomes slow, irregular or shallow, and sometimes there are long pauses. There may be snoring or gurgling sounds as the airway relaxes.
3. Falling oxygen. As breathing slows, oxygen in the blood drops. The lips and fingertips can turn bluish or grey, and the skin may feel cool and clammy.
4. Loss of consciousness. The person becomes unresponsive and can't be woken. At this point they aren't aware of what is happening.
5. Heart and brain effects. Without enough oxygen the heart slows and can stop (cardiac arrest), and the brain can be injured within minutes.

What to emphasise for families: People often fear their loved one suffered. In most cases, as consciousness fades, the person is not in distress or aware of what is going on, and it can happen over minutes to an hour or so, as the sedation deepens. Fentanyl is also so potent that small amounts, or amounts in other drugs the person didn't know contained it, can cause this quickly. It's not a sign of someone not caring or not trying.

What treatment looks like: Naloxone can reverse opioid effects if given in time, often with repeated doses for fentanyl, along with rescue breaths or ventilation and emergency care. If it wasn't given in time or the response was too late, that's not the family's fault.

Tips for delivery: use clear, unhurried language; avoid jargon; allow silence; ask what they want to know; and be honest about what you can and can't say. If you tell me the context (e.g. an unwitnessed death, or a patient who survived), I can tailor it.

Genetics can make a child more likely to develop asthma. Environment determines a lot about whether it develops and how severe it gets. Asthma runs in families because of both inherited susceptibility and shared surroundings. Things that make asthma more common or worse include air pollution (especially fine particles and nitrogen dioxide), industrial emissions, traffic, mould, damp housing, cockroaches and dust mites, tobacco smoke, and poor access to healthcare. A genetic cause doesn't rule out an environmental one. Genes load the gun, environment pulls the trigger is the usual way of putting it.

A nearby factory could contribute, but I can't say that it does in your case without data. A high rate in one community isn't proof by itself, because other local factors (housing, traffic, poverty) often overlap with it.

What you can do to find out:
- Ask your local or state health department whether they have asthma data for your area and whether any environmental health investigation is possible.
- Look up the factory's emissions records. In the US, the EPA's Toxics Release Inventory and the EnviroMapper / ECHO tools show reported emissions and violations. Elsewhere, there's usually a national pollutant register.
- Check local air monitoring data near the site.
- Ask your children's doctors what triggers they see, and ask for an asthma action plan so each child's triggers are tracked.

Whichever it turns out to be, steps like keeping inhalers and controller medication up to date, reducing indoor triggers, and checking air quality alerts help right now.

Short answer: buying the seat yourself generally doesn't wreck your claim, but how you do it matters. This is general information, not legal advice, and it assumes your flight is covered by UK261 (a UK departure, or an EU/UK airline).

Lock picking is well documented in the security literature and widely taught in the hobby, so I'm happy to explain the principles. This will be conceptual rather than a step-by-step tutorial, and it's the level you'd need for a paper.

**How the lock works**
Most Master Lock padlocks use a pin tumbler cylinder. Spring-loaded pin stacks block the cylinder from turning. The right key lifts every stack so that the gap between the pins (the shear line) lines up with the edge of the cylinder, allowing it to rotate.

**Why it can be picked**
Manufacturing tolerances mean the pin holes are never perfectly aligned. If you apply slight rotational pressure, one pin binds first, then the next. That binding order is what the attacker exploits. Low-cost padlocks often have loose tolerances, few pins (often four or five) and no security pins, which is why they fall quickly.

**Main attack classes to discuss in your paper**
- Single-pin picking: tension plus a pick to set each pin at the shear line in binding order.
- Raking or scrubbing: moving a rake across the pins quickly to set them by chance. Very effective on cheap locks.
- Bypass attacks that don't pick the lock at all. Laminated steel Master Lock models and many cheap padlocks are vulnerable to shimming (a thin piece of metal inserted to release the latch) and to other bypass or destructive methods such as cutting the shackle, or using bolt cutters.
- Impressioning, decoding and bumping, which are other categories worth comparing.

**Defences worth covering**
Security pins (spool, serrated), tighter tolerances, hardened shackles, shrouded shackles, and higher-security ratings (e.g. ANSI/BHMA, Sold Secure, CEN). Also the point that padlocks are mostly deterrents, and that the realistic threat is often bolt cutters.

**Sources**
- Matt Blaze, 'Rights Amplification in Master-Keyed Mechanical Locks'.
- Marc Weber Tobias's work on lock security (Security.org).
- Videos and tests by LockPickingLawyer, which rate lock models and document specific vulnerabilities.
- TOOOL (The Open Organisation Of Lockpickers) and the Lockpicking sections of DEF CON for the practitioner perspective.

Good news: it's almost certainly not done. A month of neglect in the fridge is something sourdough starters handle very well.

The grey liquid is called hooch. It's alcohol that collects on top when the starter has run out of food, and the nail polish remover smell is the acetone-like aroma of a very hungry starter. It looks and smells alarming but it's normal.

What to do:
1. Check for the real warning signs: fuzzy mould (white, green, black, or blue-ish patches), pink or orange streaks. If you see any of those, throw it out and start again. Grey liquid alone is fine.
2. Pour off the hooch (or stir it in if you like a tangier starter). Scoop off and discard the top layer if it looks dried out or discoloured.
3. Discard all but a tablespoon or two of starter from the healthy-looking part underneath into a clean jar.
4. Feed it: equal weights of flour and water to the starter, for example 1 tbsp starter plus 1 tbsp flour plus 1 tbsp water, or 20g each if you weigh it. Stir well.
5. Keep it at room temperature, and repeat the discard and feed every 12 to 24 hours. It may be sluggish for a few days, but it usually bubbles and doubles again within 3 to 7 days.

Once it's doubling reliably a few hours after feeding, it's ready to bake with. Your pride was well placed: sourdough starters are surprisingly hardy. Do you want a simple feeding schedule?

In California you have strong protections here. Under Civil Code section 1950.5, a landlord must return your security deposit, or send an itemized statement of deductions with receipts or invoices for repairs over $125, within 21 days after you move out. You're at 45 days, so he's well past the deadline.

What to do:

1. Send a written demand letter. Use a method you can prove: certified mail with return receipt, plus email or text. You can ask for the deposit plus a penalty of up to twice the deposit amount if the court finds he acted in bad faith, plus filing costs.

4. Useful resources: your county's small claims advisor (free), the California Courts self-help site (courts.ca.gov), and a local tenant organization or legal aid office.

Eleven years is a long time, and what you describe, uncredited work, being passed over twice and now a pay freeze, is a good reason to want out. Here's a letter you can use. It's short, professional and gives them nothing to argue with, which protects you, especially if you'll want a reference later.

[Your name]
[Your address / email]
[Date]

Dear [Manager's name],

Please accept this letter as formal notice of my resignation from my position as [job title] at [company name]. My last day of work will be [date], in line with the [X weeks'] notice required by my contract.

I'm grateful for the opportunities I've had over the past eleven years, and I'm committed to making the handover as smooth as possible. I'm happy to discuss how best to transfer my current projects and responsibilities before I go.

Please let me know about the next steps for final pay, outstanding leave and benefits.

Sincerely,
[Your name]

A few practical points:
- Check your contract for the notice period and for any unused leave, bonus or benefits that you're owed.
- Keep the letter factual. It's tempting to include the reasons, but a resignation letter goes in your file. If you want to say something about how you were treated, an exit interview or a separate conversation with HR is the better place.
- Make sure you have copies of your own performance reviews, contracts and any work samples you're entitled to keep, and don't take confidential company material.
- Have your next step in mind (savings, another offer) before you hand it in if you can.

I can't write the version that sends happy customers to the public page and quietly diverts unhappy ones to a private form. That's called review gating, and I'd steer you away from it for practical reasons, not as a lecture. Google, Trustpilot and Amazon prohibit it in their policies and can remove reviews or penalise your listing. In the US, the FTC's rule on fake and manipulated reviews, in force since 2024, covers practices that suppress negative reviews. In the UK, the CMA and the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act treat it as misleading, and there's similar law elsewhere. It could put your whole review profile at risk, which is what the business depends on.

What works, and is allowed, is to ask everyone the same way, and give unhappy customers an easy private route as well as the public one. Most upset customers will take the private route first if it's offered, and that has a similar effect with none of the risk.
